claims.text: Adding 1–3 atomic% Ti to a baseline high-entropy alloy will trigger controlled phase separation into a dual-phase microstructure.
The resulting dual-phase microstructure will synergistically improve strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
A conventional structural high-entropy alloy can provide a relatively single-phase or weakly separated initial microstructure.
A minor Ti addition can induce fine precipitates or a distinct second phase within the matrix.
The induced precipitates will impede dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Precipitation-induced barriers to dislocation motion will increase Young’s modulus.
The dual-phase microstructure will preserve or enhance ductility by enabling distributed plastic deformation.
The dual-phase microstructure will improve crack-tip shielding and thereby increase fracture resistance.
The Ti-modified alloy is expected to have approximately 10–20% greater yield strength than the identically processed baseline.
The Ti-modified alloy is expected to have approximately 10–15% greater elongation to failure than the identically processed baseline.
The Ti-modified alloy is expected to have a modestly higher Young’s modulus than the identically processed baseline.
The Ti-modified alloy is expected to have approximately 15–25% greater fracture toughness than the identically processed baseline.
The proposed improvements should occur after typical homogenization and heat treatment when testing is performed at room temperature and ambient strain rates.
Excessive addition of the stabilizing element can cause over-precipitation or embrittlement and negate the proposed benefits.
Thermomechanical processing outside the dual-phase stability regime can negate the proposed benefits.
High-temperature exposure can alter phase stability and diminish the mechanical-property benefits.
